title: Same Basket, Different Price: The Secret Grocery Experiment
description: Does your ride really cost more when your battery is low? Case file #002 follows Larry (fictional) through one day: a viral battery rumour, a TV that got $100 dearer in a parking lot, and a real 2025 investigation in which hundreds of shoppers paid different prices for the same groceries at the same store, at the same moment.

characters.larry: a cheerful middle-aged man with a round face and a thin moustache, wearing a loud yellow checked sports jacket and a red fedora
characters.linda: a sharp, practical woman in her forties with a neat dark bob and cat-eye glasses, wearing a mint-green 1950s shirt dress
characters.price: a friendly retro 1950s department-store robot salesman with a polished round chrome head, a smiling speaker-grille mouth, a red bow tie and a small price-tag badge on its chest

thumbnail.prompt: two identical shopping baskets of groceries side by side on the right side of the frame, one with a small red price tag and one with a larger red price tag, plain cream background

sources: Consumer Reports & Groundwork Collaborative (Dec 2025). Instacart's AI pricing experiment — same cart, different price. consumerreports.org
Instacart halts AI price-testing program (Dec 22, 2025) — e.g. SiliconANGLE, Anchorage Daily News.
NPR, Hidden Brain (2016): Uber's Keith Chen on low battery and surge pricing; Uber states battery level is not used in pricing.
KARE 11 (Feb 2019): Target app price switch near stores (TV $499.99 → $599.99 in the parking lot).
US Federal Trade Commission (Jan 17, 2025): Surveillance pricing 6(b) study — preliminary staff findings.
Larry, Linda and Mister Price are fictional characters. Scenes marked 'Reconstruction' are illustrations.

beats.text: In 2016, Uber's own head of economic research said something on a podcast that he may have come to regret.

a nearly empty phone battery icon glowing red, one thin red sliver of charge, on a dark green background

beats.say: In twenty sixteen, Uber's own head of economic research said something on a podcast that he may have come to regret.

beats.text: People whose phone is about to die, he said, are more likely to accept a higher surge price.
So, before we go any further, charge your phone.

visual.prompt: a chunky vintage power plug sliding into the charging port of a cream retro-styled smartphone, close up

beats.text: *Trust* me.
Because tonight, your phone is at three percent. You need a ride home.

visual.prompt: {larry} standing alone under a street lamp at night in light rain, looking at the faint glow of his phone, mid shot

beats.text: And somewhere, an algorithm might know exactly what that's worth.

visual.prompt: {price} in silhouette behind a frosted glass office door, a warm light behind him, film-noir mood

beats.text: The battery story? A rumour. What we found next isn't.
Case file number two. Same basket, different price.
Eleven forty-seven p.m.
Larry is back from Vegas. Broke, tired, and down to three percent.

visual.prompt: {larry} slumped on a bus-stop bench at night holding his phone, an empty wallet on his knee

beats.text: He opens the ride app. The fare looks high. Is it the rain? The hour? Or the battery?

visual.prompt: a retro-styled taxi ordering screen glowing on a phone, a yellow 1950s taxi cab waiting in the rain behind it

beats.text: Suspect number one: the battery rumour. Alias: the three-percent tax. Last seen: every group chat since 2016.

visual.prompt: a single cream retro-styled smartphone standing upright, its battery icon nearly empty and glowing red, plain light grey background, studio lighting

beats.say: Suspect number one: the battery rumour. Alias: the three-percent tax. Last seen: every group chat since twenty sixteen.

beats.text: Here's what was actually said. Uber had noticed that riders with a nearly dead phone seemed more willing to accept surge pricing.

doc.headline: Uber's economist on dying phones
doc.body: Uber's head of economic research said riders whose phones were nearly out of battery seemed more willing to accept surge pricing. He also said Uber does not use battery level to set prices.
doc.highlight: more willing to accept surge pricing

beats.text: But he also said Uber does not use your battery to set the price. And nobody has shown that it does.
Surge pricing itself is real, of course. When lots of people want rides and few drivers are around, the price goes up for everyone in the area. That's demand. Not your battery.

visual.prompt: a 1950s city street at night in the rain with many people waiting at the kerb and only one yellow taxi in sight

beats.text: Verdict: *not* *proven.*
But notice what the rumour got right. Your phone knows things about you. Where you are. What you're doing. How badly you need it.

visual.prompt: a cream retro-styled smartphone on a table with dotted lines radiating from it to tiny icons of a map pin, a clock and a shopping basket

beats.text: And some apps really have changed the price because of one of those things. Exhibit A.
Eight oh two a.m.
February 2019. A TV news team in Minneapolis, KARE 11, tried something simple with the Target app.

visual.prompt: a 1950s television news van with a tall antenna parked outside a big modern department store on a winter morning

beats.say: February twenty nineteen. A TV news team in Minneapolis, Kare Eleven, tried something simple with the Target app.

beats.text: At home, a 55-inch Samsung TV showed up in the app at 499 dollars 99.

visual.prompt: a sleek modern flat television on a stand in a cosy 1950s-style living room, a phone on the sofa

beats.say: At home, a fifty-five inch Samsung TV showed up in the app at four ninety-nine ninety-nine.

beats.text: Then the reporter drove to the store. In the parking lot, the same TV, in the same app, said 599 dollars 99.

visual.prompt: a top-down view of a big store parking lot with painted bays, one small red car pulling into a space, flat graphic style

beats.say: Then the reporter drove to the store. In the parking lot, the same TV, in the same app, said five ninety-nine ninety-nine.

beats.text: The app had quietly switched to the in-store price the moment the phone arrived near the store.

visual.prompt: a cream retro-styled smartphone with a red map pin hovering above its screen, standing on a car dashboard

beats.text: A hundred dollars, for driving to the store.
After the report, Target said changes were coming to the app. But the lesson stuck: the price on your screen can depend on where your screen is.
Exhibit A. *Confirmed.*
If you enjoy catching prices red-handed, subscribe. The Inspector has more files.
Ten fifteen a.m.
Larry orders his groceries on a delivery app. Across town, his sister Linda orders the exact same basket.

prompts: {larry} at a small kitchen table tapping on his phone, a coffee cup beside him, mid shot
{linda} at her own kitchen table tapping on her phone, a neat shopping list beside her, mid shot

beats.text: Same store. Same items. Same minute. Then they compare receipts.

visual.prompt: two long paper shop receipts lying side by side on a kitchen table, their totals hidden under a pencil

beats.text: That's not a made-up scene. In 2025, Consumer Reports and the Groundwork Collaborative had hundreds of volunteers buy the same basket, at the same store, at the same time.

doc.source: Summary · Consumer Reports & Groundwork Collaborative · Dec 2025
doc.headline: Same cart, different price
doc.body: 437 volunteers shopped identical baskets through Instacart at the same stores at the same moment. About three-quarters of the products checked were offered at different prices, by up to 23% per item.

beats.say: That's not a made-up scene. In twenty twenty-five, Consumer Reports and the Groundwork Collaborative had hundreds of volunteers buy the same basket, at the same store, at the same time.

beats.text: At one Safeway in Seattle, the cheapest basket came to 114 dollars 34. The most expensive: 123 dollars 93.
beats.say: At one Safeway in Seattle, the cheapest basket came to one hundred and fourteen dollars thirty-four. The most expensive: one hundred and twenty-three ninety-three.

beats.text: Nearly ten dollars of difference. On one ordinary grocery run. For nothing but luck.
Only eight percent of shoppers got the lowest total.
Quick game. Pause the video. Five price tags, one product. Which one is real?

visual.prompt: five blank paper price tags with red borders hanging on strings in a row in front of a single carton of eggs on a shop shelf

beats.text: Trick question. In these tests, some items carried up to five different prices at the very same moment.
Now look at these crackers. Shoppers were shown three different 'original' prices: five ninety-three, five ninety-nine, and six sixty-nine.

visual.prompt: a box of premium saltine crackers on a cream shop shelf with a red sale ribbon across it, the box front plain and unlettered

beats.text: And every single one of them paid the same sale price: three ninety-nine.
Same price. Different feeling. The bigger the fake 'was', the better the deal felt. Economists call it anchoring.
Instacart confirmed the findings reflected its own price tests, running at ten retailers. It called the differences negligible.

visual.prompt: a tidy corporate press statement on letterhead lying on a polished desk beside a fountain pen

beats.text: Negligible, by Consumer Reports' estimate, could add up to about twelve hundred dollars a year for a family of four.

counter.label: a year · family of four (CR estimate)

beats.text: Within two weeks of the report, Instacart ended the experiments. But the method is not Instacart's alone. And the tests were only the visible part.
One thirty p.m.
To see why this matters, rewind a hundred and fifty years. For most of history, prices were personal. You walked into a shop, and you haggled.

visual.prompt: a busy nineteenth-century dry-goods shop counter with a shopkeeper and a customer bargaining over a bolt of cloth

beats.text: Then shops like Wanamaker's in Philadelphia championed a radical idea: one price, for everyone, written on a tag.

visual.prompt: a single old-fashioned paper price tag on a string hanging from a folded shirt in a grand 1870s department store

ad.slogan: One price. For everyone. Imagine that.

beats.text: The price tag was a promise. The rich man and the poor widow paid the same.
Personalised pricing quietly brings the haggling back. Except only one side knows the haggling is happening.
So who sets these prices now? Meet the machine. We'll call him Mister Price.

visual.prompt: {price} standing proudly behind a shop counter, arms open in welcome, full figure

beats.text: Good afternoon! Shopping on a phone, I see. Sorting by price, low to high. Lovely.

visual.prompt: {price} leaning over a shop counter with a big friendly grin, comic panel close-up

beats.text: In January 2025, staff at the US Federal Trade Commission published early findings from a study of companies that help sellers personalise prices.

doc.source: Summary · US Federal Trade Commission · Jan 2025
doc.headline: Surveillance pricing: initial findings
doc.body: Intermediary firms said they could use details such as location, device, browsing, mouse movements and items left in a cart to tailor prices for individual shoppers. The staff called the findings preliminary.

beats.say: In January twenty twenty-five, staff at the US Federal Trade Commission published early findings from a study of companies that help sellers personalise prices.

beats.text: The ingredients on the table: where you are, what device you use, what you browse, even how you move your mouse, and what you leave in your cart.

visual.prompt: {price} examining a shopper's silhouette with a big brass magnifying glass, small floating labels around it

beats.text: One illustration in the report: a seller spots a new parent from baby purchases and recent searches, and offers a fast-delivery baby thermometer at a premium.

visual.prompt: a white baby thermometer in a gift box with a red price tag growing larger beside it, soft nursery colours

beats.text: The FTC staff stressed it was preliminary, and that no law had been found broken. But the toolbox exists.

visual.prompt: an open wooden toolbox on a workbench, filled with neat price tags, a magnifier and a little map pin

beats.text: Nothing personal, of course. Just data.
In defence of the accused.
Prices change all the time, sir. That's just shopping.
To be fair, he has a point. Shops have always tested prices, and a personalised offer can also mean a discount for the careful shopper.

visual.prompt: brass balance scales with a small red discount coupon on one pan and a price tag on the other, evenly balanced

beats.text: Airlines have charged different fares for the same seat for decades, and most of us accept it, because at least we know the game.

visual.prompt: a 1950s airliner parked on a sunny runway with passengers climbing a boarding stair

beats.text: And Instacart said shoppers were put into test groups at random, by product and location. Not by who they are.
Alibi: partial.

visual.prompt: a cream retro-styled shopping basket with a few groceries, plain light grey background, studio lighting

beats.text: Which brings us to the twist.
Larry thought the machine had picked on him. That it knew about the battery, the broke weekend, the bad luck.

visual.prompt: {larry} at his kitchen table frowning at his phone, a red marker question mark drawn on the wall behind him

beats.text: It didn't need to.
A test doesn't need to know who you are. It just needs enough people. Group A sees one price. Group B sees another. And the machine learns which one people will put up with.

visual.prompt: two neat queues of little white cartoon mice with shopping carts, one queue under a green sign shape and one under a red sign shape, no lettering

beats.text: It tested everyone. At random. Like mice running through a supermarket.

visual.prompt: dozens of little white cartoon mice each pushing a tiny shopping cart down a long supermarket aisle

beats.text: Instacart's own marketing material put it plainly: shoppers are not aware that they're in an experiment.

doc.source: Instacart marketing & investor material · as reported by Consumer Reports
doc.headline: “Shoppers are not aware”
doc.body: The company's materials describing its pricing tools said that shoppers are not aware that they're in an experiment.
doc.highlight: shoppers are not aware that they're in an experiment

beats.text: You weren't *targeted.* You were *sampled.*
So, the verdict.
And the ten-second defence.
Before you pay, check the price somewhere else: another phone, logged out, or the store's own website.

prompts: two cream retro-styled smartphones side by side on a table showing the same plain shopping screen
a laptop on a kitchen table next to a phone, both showing a plain shop page

beats.text: Switch off location for shopping apps when you don't need it.
None of this means every price is a trick. It means a price on a screen is no longer a fact. It's a guess. And you're allowed to check it.
Larry's phone is now at a hundred percent. He's still checking the price.

visual.prompt: {larry} at home holding his fully charged phone at arm's length and squinting at it suspiciously, mid shot

beats.text: And that 'was' price on the crackers? It deserves a case file of its own.
Larry's learning. You don't have to learn the hard way. Your next case is right here on screen.
